title: I Spy
full_review:
The 1960s TV series never looked so good until the movie version of "I Spy" (Columbia) came out. The movie is all sound and fury, signifying nothing less than Hollywood's bankruptcy of creativity.

When a U.S. superweapon, a reconnaissance aircraft that can morph into invisibility, falls into the villainous hands of boxing fan Gundars (a glowering Malcolm McDowell), special agent Alex Scott (Owen Wilson) is assigned to recover it in Budapest and fly it home. He's jazzed to be working with a would-be girlfriend, agent Rachel (Famke Janssen), but bummed to be teamed with ultracocky boxing champ Kelly Robinson (Eddie Murphy) in order to get near Gundars.

Predictably, Scott and Robinson are like oil and water.

The duo's bickering and the mayhem that follows, with its crazed chases and stale shootouts, are what pass for comedy. But, as directed by Betty Thomas, motormouth Murphy and wimpy Wilson only exemplify how tired the odd-couple buddy formula has become. Robinson, who always refers to himself in the third person -- even partner Scott finds that irritating -- wisecracks at super speed but his talky exchanges with Scott simply aren't very funny.

And so we have them racing and chasing around Budapest in a car, truck, hot-air balloon -- even a funicular -- with bullets flying but viewers' patience vanishing. The choreographed fisticuffs also take on a nasty edge when the crotch area is a prime target. However, it's all such a fantasy the stylized violence never seems realistic; it's just a relief when it's all over. By comparison, the TV series with Robert Culp and Bill Cosby, on which this jumble is based, looks like a model of wit and sophistication.

The best thing about this charmless movie is seeing the streets and monuments of Budapest, which looks appealingly old-world European.

"I Spy" may be a blockbuster and the first of a franchise, but let's hope not.

Due to frequent stylized violence, a sexually suggestive scene, some crude expressions and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
